\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}

A recurring situation in computational mathematics is this. A universal statement
$\forall n \ge 1,\ p(n)$ resists proof; a decision procedure for $p$ exists; and
so one runs the procedure on $1,2,\dots,N$ for the largest $N$ affordable. The
Collatz conjecture has been checked past $2^{68}$, Goldbach past
$4\times 10^{18}$. Everyone agrees this is \emph{evidence}. Almost nobody says
precisely what it is evidence \emph{of}.

This paper answers that question exactly: the logical strength of a certificate
(\S3), the precise structural supplement that upgrades it to a proof (\S4), and
how much a fixed budget of verified computation can be made to cover when the
supplement is unavailable (\S5--\S6). \S7 closes with a dichotomy in the language
of statistical learning that explains both halves at once.

\subsection{Notation}

$\Nat$ denotes the non-negative integers; a \emph{predicate} is a map
$p : \Nat \to \bools$. The classical Collatz map is $\mathrm{col}(n) = n/2$ for
$n$ even and $3n+1$ for $n$ odd; the \emph{accelerated map} is
\[
  T(n) = \begin{cases} n/2, & n \text{ even},\\ (3n+1)/2, & n \text{ odd}.\end{cases}
\]
We write $f^{[k]}$ for the $k$-fold iterate.

\section{A calculus of bounded checks}

\begin{definition}[Bounded check]
For a predicate $p$ define, by recursion on the \emph{length},
\[
  \Chk(p,\ell,0) = \mathrm{true}, \qquad
  \Chk(p,\ell,m+1) = p(\ell) \wedge \Chk(p,\ell+1,m),
\]
and set the \emph{window check} $C_p(\ell,h) = \Chk(p,\ell,h+1-\ell)$ with
truncated subtraction, so an empty window ($h<\ell$) succeeds.
\end{definition}

Recursion on length rather than on the endpoint keeps evaluation linear in the
number of inputs and independent of their magnitude.

\begin{theorem}[Reflection bridge]\label{thm:reflect}
For all $\ell,m$,
$\Chk(p,\ell,m) = \mathrm{true}$ iff $p(k)$ holds for all $k$ with
$\ell \le k < \ell+m$; consequently $C_p(\ell,h) = \mathrm{true}$ iff $p(k)$
holds for all $\ell \le k \le h$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $m$. The base case is vacuous quantification. In the step,
$\Chk(p,\ell,m+1)$ splits as $p(\ell)$ and $\Chk(p,\ell+1,m)$; the inductive
hypothesis converts the second conjunct, and the two directions follow by a case
split on whether $k=\ell$.
\end{proof}

Thus a successful check loses no information and invents none: \emph{soundness}
(from $C_p(\ell,h)$ and $\ell\le k\le h$ infer $p(k)$) and \emph{completeness}
(any true bounded statement is certified) both hold.

\begin{theorem}[Splitting law]\label{thm:split}
$\Chk(p,\ell,m+m') = \Chk(p,\ell,m) \wedge \Chk(p,\ell+m,m')$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Gluing]\label{cor:glue}
If $\ell \le \mathrm{mid}+1$ and $\mathrm{mid} \le h$ then
$C_p(\ell,h) = C_p(\ell,\mathrm{mid}) \wedge C_p(\mathrm{mid}+1,h)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $m$ using associativity of conjunction; the corollary rewrites
$h+1-\ell$ as $(\mathrm{mid}+1-\ell)+(h+1-(\mathrm{mid}+1))$, valid under the
stated inequalities.
\end{proof}

This law makes divide-and-conquer certification \emph{correct rather than merely
plausible}: a certificate for a long interval is a pair of certificates for
adjacent subintervals. It licenses chunking, parallelism, and resumption.
Certificates also restrict to subwindows and extend one step to the right given
a single new verification.

\begin{theorem}[Implementation independence]
$\Chk(p,\ell,m)$ equals the conjunction of $p$ over the list
$[\ell,\ell+1,\dots,\ell+m-1]$ and over the corresponding array.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}
$\FirstFail(p,\ell,0)=\bot$, and $\FirstFail(p,\ell,m+1) = \FirstFail(p,\ell+1,m)$
if $p(\ell)$, else $\ell$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Extraction]
$\FirstFail(p,\ell,m)=\bot$ iff $\Chk(p,\ell,m)$; and if
$\FirstFail(p,\ell,m)=k$ then $\ell \le k < \ell+m$ and $p(k)$ is false. Hence a
failed window check yields an explicit counterexample.
\end{theorem}

\section{The exact insufficiency of finite evidence}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{truncation} of $p$ at $N$ is $\tau_N p(k) = p(k) \wedge (k \le N)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:trunc}
$\tau_N p$ agrees with $p$ on $[0,N]$ and is false above $N$. Hence
$C_{\tau_N p}(\ell,N) = C_p(\ell,N)$ for every $\ell$, while
$\tau_N p(N+1) = \mathrm{false}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Pointwise agreement is immediate. For the certificate equality, split on whether
$C_p(\ell,N)$ holds: if it does, apply completeness to pointwise agreement; if
not, extract a counterexample and observe the same point defeats the truncated
check.
\end{proof}

Truncation is \emph{evidence-preserving sabotage}: invisible inside the certified
window, fatal immediately outside it.

\begin{theorem}[No finite bound is sound]\label{thm:notsound}
For every $N$ there is a predicate $q$ with $C_q(1,N)=\mathrm{true}$ and
$\neg\,\forall n\ge 1,\ q(n)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $q = \tau_N(\mathrm{true})$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Diagonal form]
There is no $N$ such that, for all predicates $p$, $C_p(1,N)$ implies
$\forall n \ge 1,\ p(n)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proposition}
For every $p$ and $N$ there is $q$ agreeing with $p$ on $[0,N]$ with $q(N+1)$
false and $q(N+2)$ true: certification constrains nothing about untouched inputs,
in either direction.
\end{proposition}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{version space} of $p$ at $N$ is
$V(p,N) = \{\, q : \Nat \to \bools \mid q(k)=p(k) \text{ for } 1\le k\le N \,\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Grafting]
For $f:\Nat\to\bools$ set $E_{p,N}(f)(k) = p(k)$ if $k\le N$ and
$f(k-(N+1))$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}
$E_{p,N}(f) \in V(p,N)$ for every $f$, and $E_{p,N}$ is injective.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Membership is by construction; evaluating $E_{p,N}(f)$ at $m+N+1$ recovers
$f(m)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Continuum theorem]\label{thm:continuum}
For every $p$ and $N$, $\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0} \le |V(p,N)|$. In particular
$V(p,N)$ is infinite.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$E_{p,N}$ injects $\bools^{\Nat}$, of cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$, into $V(p,N)$.
\end{proof}

Cardinality is coarse, and that is the point: finite evidence does not reduce
even the cardinality of the surviving hypothesis space.

\begin{theorem}[No finite sample determines a hypothesis]
For every finite $S \subseteq \Nat$ and every $p$ there is $q \ne p$ with
$q|_S = p|_S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Pick $m = 1+\max S \notin S$ and flip the value of $p$ at $m$.
\end{proof}

Equivalently the class of all binary predicates on $\Nat$ shatters every finite
set: its VC dimension is infinite and no finite sample complexity exists.

\begin{theorem}[Monotone but never sufficient]
Evidence is monotone --- $N \le M$ and $C_p(1,M)$ imply $C_p(1,N)$ --- yet for no
$N$ is $C_p(1,N)$ equivalent to $\forall n\ge 1,\ p(n)$.
\end{theorem}

\section{Descent certificates: a sound and complete proof system}

\begin{definition}[Descent certificate]\label{def:descent}
A \emph{descent certificate} for $p$ is a pair $(N,r)$ with $N \in \Nat$ and
$r : \Nat \to \Nat$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(base)] $C_p(1,N) = \mathrm{true}$;
\item[(range)] $r(n) \ge 1$ for all $n > N$;
\item[(descent)] $r(n) < n$ for all $n > N$;
\item[(transport)] $p(r(n))$ implies $p(n)$, for all $n > N$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Soundness]
A descent certificate for $p$ proves $\forall n \ge 1,\ p(n)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Strong induction on $n$. For $n\le N$ apply soundness of the base check;
otherwise $r(n)$ is a smaller positive integer, the induction hypothesis gives
$p(r(n))$, and transport gives $p(n)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness]\label{thm:complete}
If $\forall n \ge 1,\ p(n)$ then $p$ admits a descent certificate. Hence $p$ has
a descent certificate if and only if $\forall n \ge 1,\ p(n)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $N=1$ and $r \equiv 1$: the base check is the single instance $p(1)$, range
and descent are immediate for $n>1$, and transport holds because $p(n)$ holds
outright.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} is easy to prove and not easy to over-interpret: the
schema ``verify a finite window, then exhibit a well-founded reduction'' is a
\emph{complete} proof system for universal statements of this shape, whereas by
Theorem~\ref{thm:notsound} the schema ``verify a finite window'' is not even
sound. The delta between the two is exactly one object, the reduction $r$: the
missing ingredient in an open universal conjecture is never computational,
always structural.

\begin{theorem}[Periodic certificate]\label{thm:periodic}
Let $T>0$ with $p(n+T)=p(n)$ for all $n$. If $C_p(1,T)$ then $p(n)$ for all
$n\ge1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Instantiate Definition~\ref{def:descent} with bound $T$ and reduction
$r(n)=n-T$; transport is periodicity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Shift certificate]\label{thm:shift}
Let $a>0$ and suppose $N \le n$ and $p(n)$ imply $p(n+a)$. If
$C_p(N,N+a-1)$ then $p(n)$ for all $n \ge N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Strong induction on $n \ge N$: inputs in $[N,N+a-1]$ come from the base check;
for $n \ge N+a$ apply the hypothesis at $n-a \ge N$ and close under $+a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Last digits of fifth powers]
For all $n \in \Nat$, $n^5 \equiv n \pmod{10}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $p(n)$ be the decidable predicate $n^5 \bmod 10 = n \bmod 10$. Since
$(n+10)^5 \equiv n^5$ and $n+10 \equiv n$ modulo $10$, $p$ has period $10$. The
ten instances $n=1,\dots,10$ are checked directly, $n=0$ separately;
Theorem~\ref{thm:periodic} finishes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Chicken McNugget, with sharp boundary]
Every $n \ge 8$ is $3x+5y$ with $x,y \in \Nat$; $7$ is not; and the complete set
of non-representable integers is $\{1,2,4,7\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $p(n)$ be ``$\exists y \le n$ with $5y \le n$ and $3 \mid (n-5y)$'', a
bounded search equivalent to representability, closed under $n \mapsto n+3$. The
instances $8=3+5$, $9=3\cdot3$, $10=5\cdot2$ are checked, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:shift} with $N=8$, $a=3$ gives all $n\ge 8$. That $7$ is not
representable is a finite check; every $n<8$ outside $\{1,2,4,7\}$ is
$0,3,5,6$, each visibly representable.
\end{proof}

Here $7 = 3\cdot5-3-5$ is the Frobenius number of $\langle 3,5\rangle$, appearing
as the sharp boundary of the certified region.

\section{The Collatz instance: semantics, sieve, optimality}

\begin{definition}
$\Reach(n)$ means $\exists k,\ T^{[k]}(n)=1$; $\ReachCol(n)$ means
$\exists k,\ \mathrm{col}^{[k]}(n)=1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:reach}
$\Reach(T(n))$ implies $\Reach(n)$; $\Reach(1)$ holds;
$\Reach(T^{[j]}(n))$ implies $\Reach(n)$; and $n\ge1$ implies
$T^{[k]}(n)\ge1$ for all $k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Bridge to the classical map]\label{thm:bridge}
$\Reach(n)$ implies $\ReachCol(n)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
One accelerated step is one classical step ($n$ even) or two ($n$ odd), so
$T(n) = \mathrm{col}^{[m]}(n)$ with $m\in\{1,2\}$; induct on the number of
accelerated steps, composing classical iterates.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Fuelled checker]
$\ReachB(0,n)=\mathrm{false}$, and $\ReachB(f+1,n)$ is $\mathrm{true}$ if $n=1$,
$\mathrm{false}$ if $n=0$, and $\ReachB(f,T(n))$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Soundness and monotonicity]
$\ReachB(f,n)$ implies $\Reach(n)$; and $f \le g$ with $\ReachB(f,n)$ implies
$\ReachB(g,n)$.
\end{theorem}

Monotonicity lets certificates produced with different budgets be combined; a
certificate is never invalidated by rerunning with more fuel.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:mod41}
$T^{[2]}(4m+1) = 3m+1$; hence $\Reach(3m+1)$ implies $\Reach(4m+1)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$4m+1$ is odd, so $T(4m+1) = 6m+2$, which is even, so $T(6m+2)=3m+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sieve theorem]\label{thm:sieve4}
If $\Reach(n)$ holds for every $n \in [1,B]$ with $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, then
$\Reach(n)$ holds for every $n \in [1,B]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Strong induction on $n$. For $n=1$ trivial. If $n$ even, $T(n)=n/2<n$. If
$n=4m+1$ with $m \ge 1$ then $3m+1 < n \le B$, so the induction hypothesis and
Lemma~\ref{lem:mod41} apply. If $n \equiv 3$ the hypothesis applies directly.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact sieve density]\label{thm:density}
$\bigl|\{n \in [1,B] : n \equiv 3 \bmod 4\}\bigr| = \lfloor (B+1)/4 \rfloor$.
\end{theorem}

The two-step behaviour of $T$ modulo $4$ is completely explicit:
\[
  T^{[2]}(4m)=m,\quad T^{[2]}(4m+1)=3m+1,\quad T^{[2]}(4m+2)=3m+2,\quad
  T^{[2]}(4m+3)=9m+8 .
\]

\begin{theorem}[No input $\equiv 3 \bmod 4$ descends in two steps]
If $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ then $T^{[2]}(n) \ge n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$n=4m+3$ gives $T^{[2]}(n)=9m+8 > 4m+3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Everything else does]
If $n \ge 3$ and $n \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ then $T^{[2]}(n) < n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{non-descending set} at scale $k$ and bound $B$ is
$\ND(k,B) = \{ n \in [1,B] : T^{[k]}(n) \ge n \}$: exactly the inputs a scale-$k$
sieve must examine.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact scale-$2$ workload]\label{thm:workload2}
For $B \ge 2$,
\[
  \ND(2,B) = \{1,2\} \cup \{ n \in [1,B] : n \equiv 3 \bmod 4 \},
  \qquad |\ND(2,B)| = \left\lfloor \frac{B+1}{4}\right\rfloor + 2 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The two preceding theorems classify all $n \ge 3$; $1$ and $2$ are checked by
hand. The pieces are disjoint, so Theorem~\ref{thm:density} gives the count.
\end{proof}

Hence the hand-built mod-$4$ sieve is \emph{exactly optimal among residue sieves
at scale $2$}: it examines precisely the set that provably must be examined.

Running the fuelled checker inside the reflection calculus and applying
Theorems~\ref{thm:bridge} and~\ref{thm:sieve4} yields: every $n \le 20$, every
$n \le 1000$, and --- from a sieved certificate examining only the $1000$ inputs
$\equiv 3 \bmod 4$ --- every $n \le 4000$ satisfies $\ReachCol(n)$. The third
bound costs the same as the second and reaches four times further.

\begin{theorem}[Collatz evidence is not a proof]\label{thm:collatzwall}
For every fuel budget $f$ and bound $B$ there is a predicate $q$ agreeing with
the Collatz checker on $[0,B]$, producing an identical certificate on $[1,B]$,
and false at $B+1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[What is actually missing]
For every fuel budget $f$, the Collatz checker holds for all $n \ge 1$ if and
only if it admits a descent certificate.
\end{theorem}

\section{Stretching the budget: scale, stopping, and shape}

\begin{theorem}[Soundness of the scale-$k$ sieve]\label{thm:sievek}
If $\Reach(n)$ holds for every $n \in \ND(k,B)$, then $\Reach(n)$ holds for every
$n \in [1,B]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Strong induction on $n$: either $n \in \ND(k,B)$, or $T^{[k]}(n) < n$, in which
case the iterate is positive and $\le B$, so the induction hypothesis applies and
Lemma~\ref{lem:reach} lifts the conclusion.
\end{proof}

No threshold hypothesis is needed: the non-descending set absorbs the small
exceptional inputs automatically, which is why Theorem~\ref{thm:workload2}
contains $\{1,2\}$.

The parity of the first $k$ iterates of $n$ depends only on $n \bmod 2^k$, and if
that parity word has $s$ odd entries then $T^{[k]}(n) = (3^s n + c)/2^k$ for an
explicit bounded $c$. Hence $T^{[k]}(n) < n$ for all large $n$ in the class
precisely when $3^s < 2^k$.

\begin{definition}
Let $s_k(r)$ count the odd steps in the first $k$ iterations from residue $r$
modulo $2^k$. The class $r$ is \emph{non-contracting} at scale $k$ when
$2^k \le 3^{s_k(r)}$. Write $\NC_k$ for the set of such classes.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Arithmetic characterisation]
A residue $r < 2^k$ is non-contracting exactly when $2^k \le 3^{s_k(r)}$: the
real-analytic contraction condition collapses to this integer inequality.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Scale $2$]
The unique non-contracting class at scale $2$ is $r=3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The parity words from $0,1,2,3$ modulo $4$ have $s_2 = 0,1,1,2$; the inequality
$4 \le 3^s$ fails for $s \le 1$ and holds for $s=2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Workload bound]
$|\ND(k,B)| \le |\NC_k|\bigl(\lfloor B/2^k\rfloor + 1\bigr) + 2^k 4^k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Vanishing amortized certification cost]\label{thm:vanish}
For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a scale $k \ge 1$ such that, for all
sufficiently large $B$, $|\ND(k,B)| < \varepsilon B$ and certifying $\ND(k,B)$
certifies all of $[1,B]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Non-contraction requires $s_k(r) \ge k\log 2/\log 3 \approx 0.6309\,k$, while a
uniformly random residue modulo $2^k$ has $s_k$ distributed as a sum of $k$ fair
bits with mean $k/2$. Since $0.6309 > 1/2$, concentration gives
$|\NC_k|/2^k \to 0$; the workload bound then makes the density eventually smaller
than $\varepsilon$. Soundness is Theorem~\ref{thm:sievek}.
\end{proof}

The convergence is not monotone in $k$, since the threshold $k\log2/\log3$ crosses
integers irregularly: the density is $0.250$ at $k=2$, $0.500$ at $k=3$, $0.313$
at $k=4$; but along an arithmetic progression of scales it decreases steadily,
taking the values $0.3125, 0.2266, 0.1719, 0.1334, 0.1051$ at
$k = 4,7,10,13,16$.

The examined fraction tends to zero: certification is \emph{sublinear} in the
certified range --- and by Theorem~\ref{thm:collatzwall} still never a proof.

\begin{definition}
$\Drop(f,n)$ runs the orbit from $T(n)$ for at most $f$ accelerated steps,
succeeding as soon as it observes a value $< n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Soundness]
If $\Drop(f,n)$ succeeds then $T^{[j]}(n) < n$ for some $j \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Relative completeness]
If $T^{[j]}(n) < n$ for some $j < f$, then $\Drop(f,n)$ succeeds.
\end{theorem}

Relative completeness is what makes the substitution safe: nothing certifiable
by the expensive orbit-to-$1$ checker within the budget is lost. Empirically the
drop occurs, for inputs below $2\times10^4$, after about $3.5$ accelerated steps on
average across all inputs and about $10$ on the sieved class $3 \bmod 4$, against
about $61$ and $68$ respectively for the full orbit to $1$: a sevenfold saving on
the inputs actually examined, about eighteenfold averaged over all inputs.

\begin{theorem}[The production checker]
Define $\SD(f,n) = \mathrm{true}$ if $n \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and $\Drop(f,n)$
otherwise. If $\SD(f,n)$ holds for all $n \in [1,B]$, then $\Reach(n)$ for all
$n \in [1,B]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Balanced check]
$\Bal(p,\ell,0) = p(\ell)$ and
$\Bal(p,\ell,d+1) = \Bal(p,\ell,d) \wedge \Bal(p,\ell+2^d,d)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Shape independence]\label{thm:balanced}
$\Bal(p,\ell,d) = \Chk(p,\ell,2^d)$ for all $d,\ell$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $d$ using Theorem~\ref{thm:split} with $2^{d+1}=2^d+2^d$.
\end{proof}

The \emph{shape} of an evaluation is therefore a free parameter: two provably
equal programs, one recursing to depth $2^d$ and the other to depth $d$. Linear
evaluation of a verified window becomes infeasible around $2\times10^4$ inputs
for reasons of depth rather than time; balanced evaluation shows no such
obstruction.

\begin{theorem}[Strengthened certified bound]
Every $n \le 131072 = 2^{17}$ satisfies $\ReachCol(n)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
A single balanced window of depth $17$ starting at $1$ with the production
checker at fuel $400$; Theorem~\ref{thm:balanced} converts it to a linear window
check, the production-checker theorem to $\Reach$ on $[1,2^{17}]$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge} to the classical map.
\end{proof}

\section{The learning boundary}

\begin{definition}
$\mathcal{P}_T = \{ p : p(n+T)=p(n) \text{ for all } n \}$, the class of
$T$-periodic predicates.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Periodic extensionality]\label{thm:perext}
Let $T>0$ and $p,q \in \mathcal{P}_T$ agree on $[1,T]$. Then $p(n)=q(n)$ for all
$n \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Finite evidence identifies a periodic hypothesis]
Let $T>0$. All members of $\mathcal{P}_T \cap V(p,T)$ agree on the positive
integers: the version space is a singleton as a set of behaviours.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Two such hypotheses agree with $p$ on $[1,T]$, hence with each other; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:perext}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness of the sample size]
For every $T \ge 2$ there are distinct $p,q \in \mathcal{P}_T$ agreeing on
$[1,T-1]$ and differing at $T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $p \equiv \mathrm{true}$ and $q(k) = (k \not\equiv 0 \bmod T)$. Both have
period $T$; they agree on $[1,T-1]$ and differ at $T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Learning dichotomy]
Let $T>0$ and let the evidence be the values of a predicate at $1,\dots,T$. Then
$\mathfrak{c} \le |V(p,T)|$, while $\mathcal{P}_T \cap V(p,T)$ is a singleton on
$\Nat_{\ge1}$. The sample complexity of $\mathcal{P}_T$ is exactly $T$; the
unrestricted class has none.
\end{theorem}

Statistically: evidence is informative to the extent that the hypothesis class is
constrained. Logically: a finite window proves a universal statement to the
extent that the predicate carries a well-founded reduction. In both readings the
\emph{amount} of computation is irrelevant to the qualitative question.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmx}[Balanced window certification]
To certify a predicate on $2^d$ consecutive inputs, recursively certify the two
halves of $2^{d-1}$ and conjoin. Depth $d$, work $2^d c$ with $c$ the per-input
cost. Correctness is Theorem~\ref{thm:balanced}; Corollary~\ref{cor:glue} makes
the recursion equal to the intended conjunction.
\end{algorithmx}

\begin{algorithmx}[Sieved drop-below test]
On input $n$: if $n \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ return true. Otherwise iterate $T$ from
$T(n)$ for at most $f$ steps, returning true at the first value below $n$ and
false if the budget is exhausted. Expected cost on examined inputs is $O(1)$
accelerated steps; the examined fraction is $1/4$.
\end{algorithmx}

\begin{algorithmx}[Non-contracting class enumeration at scale $k$]
Enumerate residues $r < 2^k$, simulate $k$ steps of $T$ symbolically to record
$s_k(r)$, and retain $r$ iff $2^k \le 3^{s_k(r)}$. Cost $O(k2^k)$; the output is
exactly the residue set a scale-$k$ sieve must examine.
\end{algorithmx}

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{What ``verified to $10^{20}$'' means.}
Precisely this: the bounded statement on $[1,10^{20}]$ holds, and no more. The
version space after that computation has cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$ and contains
the truncation of the true predicate at $10^{20}$, fitting every observed bit and
failing at the next input. The intuition that large-scale verification makes a
conjecture ``probably true'' is not a theorem in the unrestricted class; it is a
Bayesian statement presupposing a prior concentrated on structured hypotheses ---
and the learning dichotomy is the precise statement that such a prior does all
the work.

\paragraph{Structure versus computation.}
Every improvement above is a theorem about what need \emph{not} be checked: the
residue sieve removes three quarters of the inputs; higher $2$-adic scales drive
the examined fraction to zero; early stopping removes the tail of each orbit, close to an order of
magnitude; and balanced evaluation removes the constraint on evaluation order. Together these
bought a factor of $6553$ in reach with no additional hardware --- and, being
theorems, at no cost in reliability.

\paragraph{Limits of the negative results.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:continuum} is a cardinality statement, deliberately coarse; it
does not preclude measure- or complexity-theoretic refinements in which finite
evidence eliminates a positive fraction of a weighted hypothesis space. Making
such a refinement precise is the most interesting direction suggested here.

\paragraph{Relation to the $3n+1$ problem.}
Nothing here bears on the truth of the conjecture. The contribution is a
reformulation: Collatz is \emph{equivalent} to the existence of a descent
certificate for its checker, hence to a well-founded reduction defined above some
finite window. Known partial results exhibit reductions valid on sets of density
tending to $1$; the gap between ``density $1$'' and ``everything'' is exactly what
Theorem~\ref{thm:vanish} quantifies and Theorem~\ref{thm:collatzwall} declares
uncrossable by computation.

\section{Future directions}

\paragraph{1. A logarithmic-depth reflection hierarchy.}
We conjecture that for every depth $d$ a balanced checker verifies $2^d$ inputs
at evaluation depth $\Theta(d)$ and time $\Theta(2^d c)$, so the reachable
certified bound is limited by \emph{time alone}, and a chunked family glued by
Corollary~\ref{cor:glue} attains any bound an unverified compiled run attains at
constant-factor slowdown. The key insight is that the failure mode of large
certificates is the \emph{shape} of the evaluation, not its size: linear
evaluation fails at $\approx 2\times10^4$ inputs at any time budget, while
balanced evaluation at the same per-input cost reached $1.3\times10^5$ with no
depth-related obstruction. The statement is falsifiable by exhibiting a depth at
which balanced evaluation fails for a reason other than time.

\paragraph{2. Optimality of the residue sieve at scale $k$.}
We conjecture the scale-$k$ sieve optimal among residue sieves: the classes that
must be examined are exactly the non-contracting ones, i.e.\ each non-contracting
class contains arbitrarily large inputs that fail to descend within $k$ steps.
Quantitatively we conjecture $|\NC_k|/2^k = \Theta(1/\sqrt{k})$ rather than the
$O(1/k)$ Chebyshev bound currently available. The key insight is that the
arithmetic characterisation reduces contraction to $2^k \le 3^{s_k(r)}$, turning
optimality into a large-deviation counting problem about parity words. The case
$k=2$ is settled: the examined set is exactly $\{1,2\}$ together with the class
$3 \bmod 4$, of size $\lfloor (B+1)/4\rfloor + 2$, because the two-step map sends
$4m+3$ to $9m+8$.

\paragraph{3. A quantitative theory of evidential value.}
Replace cardinality by measure: put a natural prior on hypothesis space and
compute the posterior mass eliminated by a certificate on $[1,N]$.

\paragraph{4. Descent certificates with non-monotone reductions.}
Weaken $r(n)<n$ to well-foundedness in another order, or to a ranking function
into a well-ordered set, so as to cover reductions such as ``descend to a smaller
$2$-adic scale''.

\paragraph{5. Certificates for other conjectures.}
The framework is conjecture-agnostic: numerical-semigroup and Frobenius-type
statements fall to shift certificates, modular statements to periodic ones, and
the interesting cases are those, like Collatz, where the reduction is conjectural
but the sieve theory is not.

\section{Conclusion}

Bounded verification has an exact logical strength, smaller than intuition
suggests and larger than pessimism allows. Smaller: no finite certificate is
sound for a universal statement, the version space after any check retains the
cardinality of the continuum, and every Collatz certificate is consistent with
failure at the next untested input. Larger: adjoining a well-founded reduction
produces a proof system that is not merely sound but complete, and simple
structural hypotheses --- periodicity, closure under a shift --- are already
reductions, converting windows of ten and three inputs into universal theorems.
Between the two lies engineering that is really mathematics, and it raised the
certified Collatz bound from $20$ to $131072$ without a faster machine. Evidence
is worthless or conclusive according to the hypothesis class, never according to
the amount of computation.

Certified Evidence: numerical demonstrations
============================================

Self-contained numerical companion to the paper
"Certified Evidence: The Exact Logical Strength of Bounded Verification,
with Application to the 3n+1 Problem".

Every demonstration below corresponds to a theorem in the paper:

  1. The reflection calculus: bounded checks, the gluing law, and

  3. Descent certificates: soundness in action, with the periodic certificate

  4. The Collatz instance: the accelerated map, the mod-4 sieve, the exact

  5. The scale-k sieve: enumeration of non-contracting residue classes via the
     integer condition  2^k <= 3^{s_k(r)},  and the vanishing density of the
     examined fraction.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
No third-party dependencies.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional, Tuple

Predicate = Callable[[int], bool]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The reflection calculus
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def check_from(p: Predicate, lo: int, length: int) -> bool:
    """Bounded conjunction of p over the `length` inputs starting at `lo`."""
    for k in range(lo, lo + length):
        if not p(k):
            return False
    return True


def check_range(p: Predicate, lo: int, hi: int) -> bool:
    """Bounded conjunction over the closed window [lo, hi]; empty windows pass."""
    return check_from(p, lo, max(0, hi + 1 - lo))


def first_fail(p: Predicate, lo: int, length: int) -> Optional[int]:
    """The least counterexample in the window, or None if the window is certified."""
    for k in range(lo, lo + length):
        if not p(k):
            return k
    return None


def demo_reflection() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. THE REFLECTION CALCULUS")
    print("=" * 74)

    def p(n: int) -> bool:
        return n * n >= n  # true everywhere

    def q(n: int) -> bool:
        return n != 37  # a planted counterexample

    print(f"  check_range(n^2 >= n, 1, 50)          = {check_range(p, 1, 50)}")
    print(f"  check_range(n != 37, 1, 50)           = {check_range(q, 1, 50)}")
    print(f"  first_fail(n != 37, 1, 50)            = {first_fail(q, 1, 50)}"
          "   <- explicit counterexample extraction")

    # Gluing law:  C(lo, hi) = C(lo, mid) AND C(mid+1, hi).
    lo, mid, hi = 1, 23, 50
    glued = check_range(p, lo, mid) and check_range(p, mid + 1, hi)
    print(f"\n  Gluing law on [{lo},{hi}] split at {mid}:")
    print(f"    whole = {check_range(p, lo, hi)},  left AND right = {glued}"
          f"   -> agree: {check_range(p, lo, hi) == glued}")

    # Gluing across many chunks: chunked / parallel / resumable certification.
    chunks: List[Tuple[int, int]] = [(1, 10), (11, 20), (21, 30), (31, 40), (41, 50)]
    chunked = all(check_range(p, a, b) for a, b in chunks)
    print(f"    five-chunk certification of [1,50]  = {chunked}"
          f"   -> agree: {chunked == check_range(p, lo, hi)}")
    print()

# 2. Insufficiency: truncation and the version space
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def truncate(p: Predicate, bound: int) -> Predicate:
    """The truncation of p at `bound`: agrees below, false above."""

    def q(k: int) -> bool:
        return p(k) and k <= bound

    return q


def demo_insufficiency() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. NO FINITE CERTIFICATE IS SOUND")
    print("=" * 74)

    def always_true(_: int) -> bool:
        return True

    print("  For each bound N, the truncation of a predicate at N produces the")
    print("  SAME certificate on [1,N] and is false at N+1.\n")
    print(f"    {'N':>10}  {'cert on [1,N] agrees':>22}  {'value at N+1':>14}")
    for bound in (20, 100, 1000, 10 ** 4, 10 ** 5):
        sabotaged = truncate(always_true, bound)
        agrees = check_range(sabotaged, 1, bound) == check_range(always_true, 1, bound)
        print(f"    {bound:>10}  {str(agrees):>22}  {str(sabotaged(bound + 1)):>14}")

    print("\n  The version space after a certificate on [1,N] is grafted from")
    print("  arbitrary behaviour beyond N; the grafting map is injective, so the")
    print("  version space has the cardinality of the continuum.  Counting the")
    print("  hypotheses distinguishable on the first m untested inputs:\n")
    print(f"    {'m untested inputs':>20}  {'distinct consistent hypotheses':>32}")
    for m in (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64):
        print(f"    {m:>20}  {2 ** m:>32}")
    print("    (as m -> oo this is 2^aleph_0 = the continuum, for every N)")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Descent certificates
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def descent_certificate_holds(
    p: Predicate, bound: int, reduce: Callable[[int], int], test_up_to: int
) -> bool:
    """Verify empirically that (bound, reduce) is a descent certificate for p
    on [1, test_up_to]: base window certified, reduction positive and strictly
    decreasing above the window, and truth transported upward."""
    if not check_range(p, 1, bound):
        return False
    for n in range(bound + 1, test_up_to + 1):
        r = reduce(n)
        if not (1 <= r < n):
            return False
        if p(r) and not p(n):
            return False
    return True


def demo_descent() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. DESCENT CERTIFICATES: FINITE WINDOWS THAT PROVE INFINITE THEOREMS")
    print("=" * 74)

    # (a) Periodic certificate:  n^5 = n (mod 10),  period 10, window of size 10.
    def last_digit_pow5(n: int) -> bool:
        return (n ** 5) % 10 == n % 10

    window_ok = check_range(last_digit_pow5, 1, 10)
    periodic_ok = all(last_digit_pow5(n + 10) == last_digit_pow5(n) for n in range(0, 500))
    print("  (a) Periodic certificate for  n^5 = n (mod 10):")
    print(f"        window [1,10] certified          : {window_ok}   (10 inputs)")
    print(f"        period 10 verified on [0,499]    : {periodic_ok}")
    print(f"        descent certificate (r(n)=n-10)  : "
          f"{descent_certificate_holds(last_digit_pow5, 10, lambda n: n - 10, 2000)}")
    print(f"        conclusion holds on [1,20000]    : "
          f"{check_range(last_digit_pow5, 1, 20000)}   <- proved from 10 inputs")

    # (b) Shift certificate: representability in the semigroup <3,5>.
    def repr35(n: int) -> bool:
        return any(5 * y <= n and (n - 5 * y) % 3 == 0 for y in range(n // 5 + 1))

    print("\n  (b) Shift certificate for the numerical semigroup <3,5>:")
    print(f"        window [8,10] certified          : "
          f"{check_range(repr35, 8, 10)}   (3 inputs)")
    print(f"        closed under n -> n+3 on [8,2000]: "
          f"{all((not repr35(n)) or repr35(n + 3) for n in range(8, 2001))}")
    print(f"        conclusion holds on [8,20000]    : {check_range(repr35, 8, 20000)}")
    gaps = [n for n in range(0, 200) if not repr35(n)]
    print(f"        complete gap set                 : {gaps}")
    print(f"        Frobenius number 3*5-3-5 = 7     : {max(gaps) == 7}")
    print()

# 4. The Collatz instance
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def accelerated(n: int) -> int:
    """T(n) = n/2 for even n, (3n+1)/2 for odd n."""
    return n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else (3 * n + 1) // 2


def classical(n: int) -> int:
    """The classical 3n+1 map."""
    return n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1


def reaches_one(fuel: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Fuelled checker: iterate T at most `fuel` times looking for 1."""
    x = n
    for _ in range(fuel):
        if x == 1:
            return True
        if x == 0:
            return False
        x = accelerated(x)
    return False


def orbit_length_to_one(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of accelerated steps until the orbit of n reaches 1."""
    steps, x = 0, n
    while x != 1:
        x = accelerated(x)
        steps += 1
    return steps


def drops_below(fuel: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Succeed as soon as the orbit of n falls strictly below n."""
    x = accelerated(n)
    for _ in range(fuel):
        if x < n:
            return True
        x = accelerated(x)
    return False


def drop_steps(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of accelerated steps until the orbit of n falls below n."""
    steps, x = 1, accelerated(n)
    while x >= n:
        x = accelerated(x)
        steps += 1
    return steps


def sieved_drop(fuel: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """The production checker: skip n outside 3 mod 4, else test drop-below."""
    if n % 4 != 3:
        return True
    return drops_below(fuel, n)


def check_pow2(p: Predicate, lo: int, depth: int) -> bool:
    """Balanced binary evaluation of the conjunction over 2^depth inputs."""
    if depth == 0:
        return p(lo)
    return check_pow2(p, lo, depth - 1) and check_pow2(p, lo + 2 ** (depth - 1), depth - 1)


def demo_collatz() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. THE COLLATZ INSTANCE: SEMANTICS, SIEVE, AND CERTIFIED BOUNDS")
    print("=" * 74)

    x, traj = 27, [27]
    while x != 1:
        x = classical(x)
        traj.append(x)
    print(f"        length {len(traj) - 1} steps, peak {max(traj)}, "
          f"first terms {traj[:10]} ...")

    print("\n  Two accelerated steps on the residue classes modulo 4:")
    for r, formula in ((0, "m"), (1, "3m+1"), (2, "3m+2"), (3, "9m+8")):
        m = 7
        n = 4 * m + r

def odd_step_count(k: int, r: int) -> int:
    """s_k(r): the number of odd steps in the first k iterations of T from r."""
    s, x = 0, r
    for _ in range(k):
        if x % 2 == 1:
            s += 1
            x = (3 * x + 1) // 2
        else:
            x = x // 2
    return s


def noncontracting_classes(k: int) -> List[int]:
    """Residues r < 2^k with 2^k <= 3^{s_k(r)}: the classes a scale-k sieve
    must examine."""
    return [r for r in range(2 ** k) if 2 ** k <= 3 ** odd_step_count(k, r)]


def demo_scale_sieve() -> None:

        s = odd_step_count(2, r)
        print(f"        r = {r}:  s_2(r) = {s},  4 <= 3^{s} = {3 ** s}"

    print(f"    {'k':>4}  {'|NC_k|':>10}  {'2^k':>10}  {'density':>10}  "

    for k in range(2, 19):

    subseq = [(k, len(noncontracting_classes(k)) / 2 ** k) for k in (4, 7, 10, 13, 16)]
    print("        " + "  ".join(f"k={k}: {d:.4f}" for k, d in subseq))

def iterate(f: Callable[[int], int], k: int, n: int) -> int:
    """The k-fold iterate of f applied to n."""
    x = n
    for _ in range(k):
        x = f(x)
    return x

def check_from(p: Predicate, lo: int, length: int) -> bool:
    """Bounded conjunction of p over the `length` inputs starting at `lo`."""
    for k in range(lo, lo + length):
        if not p(k):
            return False
    return True


def check_range(p: Predicate, lo: int, hi: int) -> bool:
    """Bounded conjunction over the closed window [lo, hi]; empty windows pass."""
    return check_from(p, lo, max(0, hi + 1 - lo))


def first_fail(p: Predicate, lo: int, length: int) -> Optional[int]:
    """The least counterexample in the window, or None if the window is certified."""
    for k in range(lo, lo + length):
        if not p(k):
            return k
    return None

def truncate(p: Predicate, bound: int) -> Predicate:
    """The truncation of p at `bound`: agrees below, false above."""

    def q(k: int) -> bool:
        return p(k) and k <= bound

    return q

def descent_certificate_holds(
    p: Predicate, bound: int, reduce: Callable[[int], int], test_up_to: int
) -> bool:
    """Verify empirically that (bound, reduce) is a descent certificate for p
    on [1, test_up_to]: base window certified, reduction positive and strictly
    decreasing above the window, and truth transported upward."""
    if not check_range(p, 1, bound):
        return False
    for n in range(bound + 1, test_up_to + 1):
        r = reduce(n)
        if not (1 <= r < n):
            return False
        if p(r) and not p(n):
            return False
    return True

def accelerated(n: int) -> int:
    """T(n) = n/2 for even n, (3n+1)/2 for odd n."""
    return n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else (3 * n + 1) // 2


def classical(n: int) -> int:
    """The classical 3n+1 map."""
    return n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1


def reaches_one(fuel: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Fuelled checker: iterate T at most `fuel` times looking for 1."""
    x = n
    for _ in range(fuel):
        if x == 1:
            return True
        if x == 0:
            return False
        x = accelerated(x)
    return False


def orbit_length_to_one(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of accelerated steps until the orbit of n reaches 1."""
    steps, x = 0, n
    while x != 1:
        x = accelerated(x)
        steps += 1
    return steps


def drops_below(fuel: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Succeed as soon as the orbit of n falls strictly below n."""
    x = accelerated(n)
    for _ in range(fuel):
        if x < n:
            return True
        x = accelerated(x)
    return False


def drop_steps(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of accelerated steps until the orbit of n falls below n."""
    steps, x = 1, accelerated(n)
    while x >= n:
        x = accelerated(x)
        steps += 1
    return steps


def sieved_drop(fuel: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """The production checker: skip n outside 3 mod 4, else test drop-below."""
    if n % 4 != 3:
        return True
    return drops_below(fuel, n)


def check_pow2(p: Predicate, lo: int, depth: int) -> bool:
    """Balanced binary evaluation of the conjunction over 2^depth inputs."""
    if depth == 0:
        return p(lo)
    return check_pow2(p, lo, depth - 1) and check_pow2(p, lo + 2 ** (depth - 1), depth - 1)

def odd_step_count(k: int, r: int) -> int:
    """s_k(r): the number of odd steps in the first k iterations of T from r."""
    s, x = 0, r
    for _ in range(k):
        if x % 2 == 1:
            s += 1
            x = (3 * x + 1) // 2
        else:

    return accelerated(accelerated(n))


def steps_to_one(n: int) -> int:

### What a computation proves, what it never proves, and exactly what closes the gap

---

## 0. A game, and a question

Pick a whole number. If it is even, halve it. If it is odd, triple it and add one. Repeat.

$$7 \to 22 \to 11 \to 34 \to 17 \to 52 \to 26 \to 13 \to 40 \to 20 \to 10 \to 5 \to 16 \to 8 \to 4 \to 2 \to 1$$

Sixteen steps, an excursion up to $52$, and collapse. Start at $27$ and the orbit climbs to $9232$ before crashing to $1$ after $111$ steps. Every number anyone has ever tried ends at $1$. The claim that **every** positive integer does is the [Collatz conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collatz_conjecture), open since the 1930s.

Now suppose someone hands you a certificate: a verified computation showing every integer from $1$ to $20$ reaches $1$. **What exactly have you learned?**

That question has a precise answer, and this page works it out in three movements:

1. **What a finite check is worth** — it is *exactly* the bounded statement, no more and no less.
2. **What it is not worth** — no finite bound is ever sound for a universal claim, and we will make that quantitative.
3. **What closes the gap** — a single extra object, and a proof system that is provably complete once you have it.

Along the way we will squeeze a fixed computational budget from a reach of $20$ to a reach of $131072$, entirely by proving theorems about what does *not* need to be checked.

---

## 1. The bounded check, and its three laws

Fix a yes/no test $p$ on the positive integers. The **bounded check** over a window is just the finite conjunction

$$C_p(\ell, h) \;=\; p(\ell) \wedge p(\ell+1) \wedge \cdots \wedge p(h).$$

Three facts about this object turn out to carry all the computational content.

> **Reflection Principle.** $C_p(\ell,h)$ is true if and only if $p(k)$ holds for every $k$ with $\ell \le k \le h$.

So a check neither loses information nor invents any: it *is* the bounded statement.

> **Gluing Law.** $C_p(\ell,h) = C_p(\ell,\mathrm{mid}) \wedge C_p(\mathrm{mid}+1,h)$.

This is why chunked, parallel and resumable certification is legitimate rather than merely plausible: a certificate for a long interval is *definitionally* a pair of certificates for adjacent pieces.

> **Extraction.** If a check fails, one can read off an explicit $k$ in the window with $p(k)$ false.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proofs</b></summary>

**Reflection.** Define the check by recursion on the *length* of the window: the empty window succeeds, and a window of length $m+1$ is $p(\ell)$ together with the window of length $m$ starting at $\ell+1$. Induct on $m$. The base case is vacuous quantification over an empty range. In the step, the inductive hypothesis converts the tail, and the two directions follow from a case split on whether $k = \ell$ or $k > \ell$.

**Gluing.** First prove the splitting law $\mathrm{Chk}(p,\ell,m+m') = \mathrm{Chk}(p,\ell,m) \wedge \mathrm{Chk}(p,\ell+m,m')$ by induction on $m$, using associativity of conjunction. Then rewrite the length $h+1-\ell$ as $(\mathrm{mid}+1-\ell) + (h+1-(\mathrm{mid}+1))$, which is valid whenever $\ell \le \mathrm{mid}+1 \le h+1$.

**Extraction.** Define the first-failure search by the same recursion; prove by induction that it returns nothing exactly when the check succeeds, and that anything it returns lies in the window and falsifies $p$.
</details>

Recursion on *length* rather than on the endpoint is not a stylistic choice: it makes the evaluation cost linear in the number of inputs and independent of their magnitude. Here is the calculus in code, together with the balanced evaluation strategy we will need in §5.

## 2. The wall

Now the bad news, and it is not a matter of degree.

> **Finite Evidence Is Never Sound.** For every bound $N$, however astronomical, there is a predicate that passes the check on $[1,N]$ and is false somewhere.

The witness is embarrassingly simple. Given any predicate $p$, its **truncation** is $\tau_N p(k) = p(k) \wedge (k \le N)$. It agrees with $p$ at every input inside the window — so it produces the *same certificate, bit for bit* — and it is false at $N+1$.

Play with it. Move the slider in the first experiment below and watch the honest predicate and its saboteur stay pixel-for-pixel identical throughout the certified region, then diverge the instant you step outside.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

The sharpened form is a statement about the **version space**: the set of hypotheses still consistent with the evidence.

> **Continuum Theorem.** After checking any predicate on $[1,N]$, the version space still has the cardinality of the continuum.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the construction</b></summary>

Given the certified prefix, graft an arbitrary function $f$ onto the tail:
$$E(f)(k) = \begin{cases} p(k), & k \le N,\\ f\bigl(k - (N+1)\bigr), & k > N.\end{cases}$$
Every $E(f)$ is consistent with the evidence, and $E$ is injective — evaluate $E(f)$ at $m + N + 1$ to recover $f(m)$. So the whole function space $\{\text{true},\text{false}\}^{\mathbb{N}}$, of cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$, injects into the version space.
</details>

Readers who have met [statistical learning theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vapnik%E2%80%93Chervonenkis_dimension) will recognise the shape: the class of all binary predicates on $\mathbb{N}$ shatters every finite set, so its VC dimension is infinite and no finite sample complexity exists. Concretely: given any finite sample and any hypothesis, flip the value at one unsampled point and you have a different hypothesis fitting the same data exactly.

This demo mounts the attack against real Collatz evidence, at five different bounds.

## 3. What closes the gap

If more computation is not the answer, what is? Exactly one object.

> **Definition (Descent Certificate).** A descent certificate for $p$ is a bound $N$, a verified check of $p$ on $[1,N]$, and a **reduction** $r$ such that for every $n > N$:
> $1 \le r(n)$, $\;r(n) < n$, and $p(r(n))$ implies $p(n)$.

> **Soundness.** A descent certificate proves $p(n)$ for every $n \ge 1$.
>
> **Completeness.** Conversely, every true universal statement of this form admits a descent certificate.

That pair of statements is the heart of the matter. "Finite check" alone is not even *sound*; "finite check $+$ descent" is **complete**. The delta between the two systems is one function.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal both proofs</b></summary>

**Soundness** is strong induction. For $n \le N$ apply the base check. For $n > N$, the value $r(n)$ is a strictly smaller positive integer, so the inductive hypothesis gives $p(r(n))$, and transport gives $p(n)$.

**Completeness** is a one-line construction: if $p$ holds universally, take $N = 1$ and $r \equiv 1$. The base check is the single instance $p(1)$; range and descent are immediate; transport holds because $p(n)$ holds outright.

The completeness proof is trivial, and that is precisely the content: it says the schema is *never* the bottleneck. Whenever a universal statement of this shape is true, a proof in the format "finite window plus well-founded reduction" exists. No third ingredient is ever required.
</details>

Two structural hypotheses that occur everywhere are already reductions:

- **Periodicity.** If $p(n+T) = p(n)$ with $T > 0$, checking $[1,T]$ proves $p$ universally. (Reduce $n$ to $n-T$.)
- **Shift closure.** If $p(n)$ implies $p(n+a)$ above $N$, checking the window $[N, N+a-1]$ of length $a$ proves $p$ for all $n \ge N$.

And these are not toys. Ten checked inputs and periodicity give
$$n^5 \equiv n \pmod{10} \quad\text{for every } n,$$
the familiar fact that fifth powers preserve last digits. Three checked inputs and shift closure give the [Chicken McNugget theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coin_problem): every $n \ge 8$ is a non-negative combination $3x + 5y$. The boundary is sharp — the complete gap set is $\{1,2,4,7\}$, and $7 = 3\cdot 5 - 3 - 5$ is the Frobenius number of $\langle 3, 5\rangle$.

## 4. Squeezing the budget, part I: structure

Return to Collatz, where nobody has a reduction and everybody has computers. Since no certificate will be a proof, the remaining question is genuinely mathematical: **how far can a fixed amount of verified computation reach?**

It helps to run the game at double speed. The **accelerated map** is
$$T(n) = \begin{cases} n/2, & n \text{ even},\\ (3n+1)/2, & n \text{ odd},\end{cases}$$
merging the guaranteed halving after an odd step into the odd step itself. One accelerated step is one or two ordinary steps, so conclusions transfer to the classical $3n+1$ rule.

Watch what two accelerated steps do to the four residue classes modulo $4$:

$$4m \mapsto m, \qquad 4m+1 \mapsto 3m+1, \qquad 4m+2 \mapsto 3m+2, \qquad 4m+3 \mapsto 9m+8.$$

Three of the four **descend**. Only $4m+3 \mapsto 9m+8$ grows.

> **Mod-4 Sieve.** To certify that every $n \le B$ reaches $1$, it suffices to certify only the inputs $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ — exactly $\lfloor (B+1)/4\rfloor$ of them.

> **Optimality.** And this cannot be improved: since $9m+8 > 4m+3$ always, *no* input congruent to $3 \bmod 4$ descends in two steps, so the sieve examines precisely the set that must be examined. The exact scale-$2$ workload on $[1,B]$ is $\lfloor (B+1)/4\rfloor + 2$.

The picture below makes the optimality visible at a glance: three residue classes sit below the descent threshold, one sits stubbornly above it at $9/4$.

{{visualization:1}}

The sieve is the $k = 2$ member of a family. At scale $k$, ask which classes modulo $2^k$ fail to descend within $k$ steps. Remarkably, the answer is a clean integer inequality.

> **Arithmetic characterisation.** A class $r$ modulo $2^k$ is *non-contracting* exactly when $2^k \le 3^{\,s_k(r)}$, where $s_k(r)$ counts the odd steps in the first $k$ iterations from $r$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal why, and why the density vanishes</b></summary>

The parity of the first $k$ iterates depends only on $n \bmod 2^k$. If the parity word has $s$ odd entries then $T^{[k]}(n) = (3^s n + c)/2^k$ for an explicit bounded $c$, so large members of the class descend exactly when $3^s < 2^k$.

At $k = 2$ the classes $0, 1, 2, 3$ have $s_2 = 0, 1, 1, 2$; the inequality $4 \le 3^s$ fails for $s \le 1$ and holds for $s = 2$. The unique non-contracting class is $3$ — the hand-built sieve, confirmed.

For general $k$, non-contraction forces $s_k(r) \ge k\log 2/\log 3 \approx 0.6309\,k$, while a uniformly random residue has $s_k$ distributed as a sum of $k$ fair coin flips, with mean $k/2$. Since $0.6309 > 1/2$, [large deviations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernoff_bound) drive the fraction of non-contracting classes to zero.
</details>

> **Vanishing Amortized Cost.** For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a scale $k$ such that, for all large $B$, the scale-$k$ sieve is sound for $[1,B]$ and examines fewer than $\varepsilon B$ inputs.

Certified checking is therefore **sublinear** in the certified range — and still, by the Continuum Theorem, worth nothing as a proof. That juxtaposition is the moral of the whole story. Here is the enumeration that computes the examined classes at any scale:

## 5. Squeezing the budget, part II: stopping early and changing shape

Two further ideas are what actually moved the number.

**Stop early.** Following an orbit all the way to $1$ costs about $60$–$70$ accelerated steps. But the strong induction never needed the orbit to reach $1$ — only to fall *below its own starting point*, after which the inductive hypothesis takes over. That happens after about $3.5$ steps on average across all inputs, and about $10$ on the harder sieved class.

Crucially the cheap test is **relatively complete**: whenever a descent exists inside the step budget, the cheap checker finds it. Nothing certifiable by the expensive checker is lost.

{{algorithm:1}}

**Change the shape.** A naive check recurses linearly along the interval, so the evaluation depth grows with the window and collapses at around $2 \times 10^4$ inputs, at *any* time budget. Replace it with balanced splitting: certify $2^d$ inputs as two halves of $2^{d-1}$. By the gluing law the value computed is provably identical — only the shape changes, and depth $d$ replaces depth $2^d$.

Put together, the reach climbs:

$$20 \;\longrightarrow\; 1000 \;\longrightarrow\; 4000 \;\longrightarrow\; 131072,$$

a factor of $6553$ over the evidence we started with, without a faster machine. Every step is a theorem about why less work suffices.

## 6. When evidence *is* conclusive

The Continuum Theorem sounds like a death sentence for empirical mathematics — but read the fine print. It is a statement about the *unrestricted* class. Restrict the class and everything inverts.

> **Learning Dichotomy.** Fix $T \ge 1$ and take as evidence the values of a predicate at $1, \ldots, T$. In the unrestricted class the version space has the cardinality of the continuum. In the class of $T$-periodic predicates it is a **singleton**: the evidence determines the hypothesis on all positive integers.

And the sample size is sharp: for every $T \ge 2$ there are two distinct $T$-periodic predicates agreeing on $[1,T-1]$, so $T-1$ samples do not suffice. The sample complexity of the periodic class is exactly $T$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the two arguments</b></summary>

**Identification.** If two $T$-periodic predicates agree on $[1,T]$, then by strong induction they agree everywhere above $0$: for $n > T$, both sides reduce to their values at $n - T \ge 1$.

**Sharpness.** Take $p \equiv \text{true}$ and $q(k) = (k \not\equiv 0 \bmod T)$. Both have period $T$; on $[1,T-1]$ we have $k \bmod T = k \ne 0$ so they agree; at $T$ they differ.
</details>

Explore the contrast in the third experiment of the "Evidence versus Proof" widget above: same evidence, continuum on one side, a single surviving hypothesis on the other.

This is the statistical shadow of the descent theorem, and the two say the same thing in different languages. *Statistically*: evidence is informative to the extent the hypothesis class is constrained. *Logically*: a finite window proves a universal statement to the extent the predicate carries a well-founded reduction. Neither ever depends on the **amount** of computation.

---

## 7. Everything at once

The complete numerical companion runs every experiment on this page end to end — the reflection calculus, the truncation attack, the descent certificates, the full Collatz ladder with exact workload accounting, the scale-$k$ enumeration, and the learning dichotomy.

{{demo:0}}

## 8. What to take away

1. **A certificate to $10^{20}$ means exactly one thing:** the bounded statement on $[1,10^{20}]$ holds. The version space afterwards has the cardinality of the continuum, and it contains a hypothesis that fits every observed bit and fails at the next input.
2. **The intuition that verification makes a conjecture "probably true" is a statement about a prior**, not a theorem — and the learning dichotomy is the precise statement that the prior, concentrated on structured classes, does all the work.
3. **Between checking and proving lies a nameable, complete proof system.** Collatz is *equivalent* to the existence of a descent certificate; the missing ingredient is a reduction function, not another decade of CPU time.
4. **Meanwhile, the engineering is real mathematics.** Reformulating what needs to be checked — by residue class, by early stopping, by evaluation shape — bought a factor of $6553$ with no new hardware, and the asymptotic version shows the examined fraction can be made arbitrarily small.

The child's game is still unsolved. But we now know, with precision, what kind of thing would solve it — and exactly what kind of thing never will.

# Certified Collatz evidence, and the exact line it cannot cross

This file instantiates the reflection kernel of `CertifiedEvidence.Core` on the
`3n+1` map of `MachineLearning.CollatzSpectral.ParityBijection`, and pushes the
certified window as far as kernel arithmetic allows.  Three things happen.

**1. Semantics, not just bits.** A fuelled Boolean checker `reachesOneB` is
proved sound for the genuine mathematical statement `∃ k, T^[k] n = 1`, and the
accelerated map `T` is bridged to the classical map `collatz`
(`reachesOne_collatz_of_T`), so the certified conclusion is about `3n+1` itself
and not about an auxiliary program.

**2. Structure beats brute force.** `sieve_mod4` proves that verifying only the
residue class `n ≡ 3 (mod 4)` verifies *everything*: even inputs halve, and
`4m+1` descends to `3m+1 < 4m+1` in two accelerated steps.  `sieveDensity`
computes the exact saving — the certified subset has cardinality `(B+1)/4`.
The certified bound therefore reaches `4000` for the price of `1000` inputs,
while the unsieved run stops at `1000`.

entire family of certificates is consistent with the failure of the conjecture
at the very next input: no bound `B`, however large, closes the gap. The
positive counterpart is `collatz_descent_certificate_iff`: the conjecture is
equivalent to the existence of a descent certificate, i.e. what is missing is
exactly a reduction function, not more computation.

|-----------------------------------|------------------------|-----------------|
| `evidence_20` (fuel 130)          | 20                     | < 1 s           |
| `evidence_1000` (fuel 130)        | 1000                   | ≈ 28 s          |

import Mathlib
import MachineLearning.CertifiedEvidence.Core
import MachineLearning.CertifiedEvidence.Insufficiency
import MachineLearning.CertifiedEvidence.Sufficiency
import MachineLearning.CollatzSpectral.DescentTheorem

namespace CertifiedEvidence

open CollatzParity

/-! ## §1. The statement being certified -/

/-- The orbit of `n` under the accelerated map reaches `1`. -/
def ReachesOne (n : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ k, T^[k] n = 1

/-- The orbit of `n` under the classical `3n+1` map reaches `1`. -/
def CollatzReachesOne (n : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ k, collatz^[k] n = 1

theorem reachesOne_of_T {n : ℕ} (h : ReachesOne (T n)) : ReachesOne n := by
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
  exact ⟨k + 1, by rw [Function.iterate_succ_apply]; exact hk⟩

theorem reachesOne_one : ReachesOne 1 := ⟨0, rfl⟩

/-- Positivity is preserved by the accelerated map. -/
theorem one_le_iterate_T : ∀ (k n : ℕ), 1 ≤ n → 1 ≤ T^[k] n := by
  intro k
  induction k with
  | zero => intro n hn; simpa using hn
  | succ k ih =>
      intro n hn
      rw [Function.iterate_succ_apply]
      exact ih (T n) (one_le_T hn)

/-- Reaching `1` from any iterate implies reaching `1` from the start. -/
theorem reachesOne_of_iterate {j n : ℕ} (h : ReachesOne (T^[j] n)) : ReachesOne n := by
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
  exact ⟨k + j, by rw [Function.iterate_add_apply]; exact hk⟩

/-- One accelerated step is one or two classical steps. -/
theorem exists_collatz_iterate_eq_T (n : ℕ) : ∃ m, collatz^[m] n = T n := by
  rw [T_eq_collatz n]
  by_cases h : n % 2 = 0
  · exact ⟨1, by simp [h]⟩
  · exact ⟨2, by simp [h, Function.iterate_succ_apply]⟩

/-- **Bridge to the classical map.** Reaching `1` under the accelerated map
implies reaching `1` under `3n+1`, so every certificate below is a certificate
about the Collatz conjecture as usually stated. -/
theorem reachesOne_collatz_of_T {n : ℕ} (h : ReachesOne n) : CollatzReachesOne n := by
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
  induction k generalizing n with
  | zero => exact ⟨0, hk⟩
  | succ k ih =>
      rw [Function.iterate_succ_apply] at hk
      obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ := ih hk
      obtain ⟨j, hj⟩ := exists_collatz_iterate_eq_T n
      exact ⟨m + j, by rw [Function.iterate_add_apply, hj]; exact hm⟩

/-! ## §2. The fuelled checker and its soundness -/

/-- The fuelled Boolean checker: iterate `T` at most `fuel` times looking for `1`. -/
def reachesOneB : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
  | 0, _ => false
  | f + 1, n => if n = 1 then true else if n = 0 then false else reachesOneB f (T n)

/-- **Soundness of the checker.** A `true` from the kernel is a mathematical
proof that the orbit reaches `1`. -/
theorem reachesOneB_sound : ∀ (f n : ℕ), reachesOneB f n = true → ReachesOne n := by
  intro f
  induction f with
  | zero => intro n h; exact absurd h (by simp [reachesOneB])
  | succ f ih =>
      intro n h
      by_cases h1 : n = 1
      · exact h1 ▸ reachesOne_one
      · by_cases h0 : n = 0
        · rw [reachesOneB, if_neg h1, if_pos h0] at h
          exact absurd h (by simp)
        · rw [reachesOneB, if_neg h1, if_neg h0] at h
          exact reachesOne_of_T (ih (T n) h)

/-- More fuel never invalidates a certificate: certificates compose across runs
with different budgets. -/
theorem reachesOneB_mono : ∀ (f g n : ℕ), f ≤ g → reachesOneB f n = true →
    reachesOneB g n = true := by
  intro f
  induction f with
  | zero => intro g n _ h; exact absurd h (by simp [reachesOneB])
  | succ f ih =>
      intro g n hfg h
      obtain ⟨g', rfl⟩ : ∃ g', g = g' + 1 := ⟨g - 1, by omega⟩
      by_cases h1 : n = 1
      · simp [reachesOneB, h1]
      · by_cases h0 : n = 0
        · rw [reachesOneB, if_neg h1, if_pos h0] at h
          exact absurd h (by simp)
        · rw [reachesOneB, if_neg h1, if_neg h0] at h ⊢
          exact ih g' (T n) (by omega) h

/-! ## §3. The mod-4 sieve: structure that quarters the work -/

theorem T_even {n : ℕ} (h : n % 2 = 0) : T n = n / 2 := by simp [T, h]

/-- Two accelerated steps take `4m+1` to `3m+1`. -/
theorem T_two_steps_mod4 (m : ℕ) : T (T (4 * m + 1)) = 3 * m + 1 := by
  have h1 : (4 * m + 1) % 2 = 1 := by omega
  have h2 : T (4 * m + 1) = 6 * m + 2 := by
    rw [T, if_neg (by omega)]
    omega
  rw [h2, T, if_pos (by omega)]
  omega

/-- Inputs `≡ 1 (mod 4)` above `1` descend strictly, so they never need checking. -/
theorem reachesOne_of_mod4_one {m : ℕ} (h : ReachesOne (3 * m + 1)) :
    ReachesOne (4 * m + 1) := by
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
  have h2 : (T^[2]) (4 * m + 1) = 3 * m + 1 := by
    simp [Function.iterate_succ_apply, T_two_steps_mod4 m]
  exact ⟨k + 2, by rw [Function.iterate_add_apply, h2]; exact hk⟩

/-- **The sieve theorem.** Certifying only the residue class `3 mod 4` inside
`[1,B]` certifies the whole interval. Even inputs halve; `4m+1` descends to
`3m+1`; the induction is on the input. -/
theorem sieve_mod4 (B : ℕ) (h : ∀ n, 1 ≤ n → n ≤ B → n % 4 = 3 → ReachesOne n) :
    ∀ n, 1 ≤ n → n ≤ B → ReachesOne n := by
  intro n
  induction n using Nat.strong_induction_on with
  | _ n ih =>
      intro hn hnB
      rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hn with rfl | hn1
      · exact reachesOne_one
      · by_cases hpar : n % 2 = 0
        · have hhalf : ReachesOne (n / 2) := ih (n / 2) (by omega) (by omega) (by omega)
          have := reachesOne_of_T (n := n)
          rw [T_even hpar] at this
          exact this hhalf
        · -- odd inputs split by their residue mod 4
          rcases (by omega : n % 4 = 1 ∨ n % 4 = 3) with h1 | h3
          · obtain ⟨m, rfl⟩ : ∃ m, n = 4 * m + 1 := ⟨n / 4, by omega⟩
            have hm : 1 ≤ m := by omega
            exact reachesOne_of_mod4_one
              (ih (3 * m + 1) (by omega) (by omega) (by omega))
          · exact h n hn hnB h3

/-- The exact size of the sieved workload: `(B+1)/4` inputs instead of `B`. -/
theorem sieveDensity (B : ℕ) :
    ((Finset.Icc 1 B).filter (fun n => n % 4 = 3)).card = (B + 1) / 4 := by
  induction B with
  | zero => decide
  | succ B ih =>
      have hins : Finset.Icc 1 (B + 1) = insert (B + 1) (Finset.Icc 1 B) := by
        ext x
        simp [Finset.mem_Icc, Finset.mem_insert]
        omega
      rw [hins, Finset.filter_insert]
      by_cases h : (B + 1) % 4 = 3
      · rw [if_pos h, Finset.card_insert_of_notMem (by simp), ih]
        omega
      · rw [if_neg h, ih]
        omega

/-! ## §4. The certificates -/

/-- The unsieved checker. -/
def collatzChecker (fuel n : ℕ) : Bool := reachesOneB fuel n

/-- The sieved checker: inputs outside `3 mod 4` are skipped outright. -/
def sievedChecker (fuel n : ℕ) : Bool := if n % 4 = 3 then reachesOneB fuel n else true

theorem sievedChecker_trivial (fuel n : ℕ) (h : n % 4 ≠ 3) : sievedChecker fuel n = true := by
  simp [sievedChecker, h]

/-- The evidence supplied with the problem statement, re-derived in the kernel. -/
theorem evidence_20 : checkRange (collatzChecker 130) 1 20 = true := by decide

/-- …and its mathematical content, for the classical `3n+1` map. -/
theorem collatz_upTo_20 (n : ℕ) (h1 : 1 ≤ n) (h2 : n ≤ 20) : CollatzReachesOne n :=
  reachesOne_collatz_of_T (reachesOneB_sound 130 n (of_checkRange evidence_20 h1 h2))

theorem evidence_1000 : checkRange (collatzChecker 130) 1 1000 = true := by decide

theorem collatz_upTo_1000 (n : ℕ) (h1 : 1 ≤ n) (h2 : n ≤ 1000) : CollatzReachesOne n :=
  reachesOne_collatz_of_T (reachesOneB_sound 130 n (of_checkRange evidence_1000 h1 h2))

theorem sieved_evidence_4000 : checkRange (sievedChecker 200) 1 4000 = true := by decide

  · exact truncate_fails _ B

`CertifiedEvidence.Insufficiency` shows the version space after finite evidence
has the cardinality of the continuum — but that is a statement about the

  space for the unrestricted class, singleton for the periodic class, at the

import Mathlib
import MachineLearning.CertifiedEvidence.Insufficiency
import MachineLearning.CertifiedEvidence.Sufficiency

/-- The hypothesis class of predicates with period `T`. -/
def PeriodicClass (T : ℕ) : Set (ℕ → Bool) := {p | ∀ n, p (n + T) = p n}

  intro n

  | _ n ih =>

      by_cases h : n ≤ T
      · exact hagree n hn h
      · push_neg at h
        have hback : n - T + T = n := by omega
        have h1 : p n = p (n - T) := by
          have hpp := hp (n - T); rwa [hback] at hpp
        have h2 : q n = q (n - T) := by
          have hqq := hq (n - T); rwa [hback] at hqq
        rw [h1, h2]
        exact ih (n - T) (by omega) (by omega)

theorem periodic_versionSpace_subsingleton {T : ℕ} (hT : 0 < T) (p : ℕ → Bool)

  rw [h₁.2 k hk hk', h₂.2 k hk hk']

    rw [truncate_fails] at this
    exact Bool.noConfusion this

def versionSpace (p : ℕ → Bool) (N : ℕ) : Set (ℕ → Bool) :=
  {q | ∀ k, 1 ≤ k → k ≤ N → q k = p k}

  simpa [extendBeyond, Nat.not_le.mpr (show N < m + N + 1 by omega),
    show m + N + 1 - (N + 1) = m by omega] using this

def accelerated(n: int) -> int:
    """T(n) = n/2 for even n, (3n+1)/2 for odd n."""
    return n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else (3 * n + 1) // 2


def classical(n: int) -> int:
    """The classical 3n+1 map."""
    return n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1


def reaches_one(fuel: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Fuelled checker: iterate T at most `fuel` times looking for 1."""
    x = n
    for _ in range(fuel):
        if x == 1:
            return True
        if x == 0:
            return False
        x = accelerated(x)
    return False


def orbit_length_to_one(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of accelerated steps until the orbit of n reaches 1."""
    steps, x = 0, n
    while x != 1:
        x = accelerated(x)
        steps += 1
    return steps


def drops_below(fuel: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Succeed as soon as the orbit of n falls strictly below n."""
    x = accelerated(n)
    for _ in range(fuel):
        if x < n:
            return True
        x = accelerated(x)
    return False


def drop_steps(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of accelerated steps until the orbit of n falls below n."""
    steps, x = 1, accelerated(n)
    while x >= n:
        x = accelerated(x)
        steps += 1
    return steps

    """The production checker: skip n outside 3 mod 4, else test drop-below."""
    if n % 4 != 3:
        return True
    return drops_below(fuel, n)

    if depth == 0:
        return p(lo)
    return check_pow2(p, lo, depth - 1) and check_pow2(p, lo + 2 ** (depth - 1), depth - 1)

    print(f"        mod-4 sieve on [1,4000]            : {sieved_4000}"
          f"   (examined {(4000 + 1) // 4})")
    balanced = check_pow2(lambda n: sieved_drop(400, n), 1, 17)
    print(f"        sieve + drop-below, balanced, 2^17 : {balanced}"
          f"   (examined {2 ** 17 // 4})")
    print(f"        => every n <= {1 + 2 ** 17 - 1} reaches 1 under 3n+1;"
          f" a {(2 ** 17) // 20}x extension of the 20-input evidence")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. The scale-k sieve and vanishing density
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def odd_step_count(k: int, r: int) -> int:
    """s_k(r): the number of odd steps in the first k iterations of T from r."""
    s, x = 0, r
    for _ in range(k):
        if x % 2 == 1:
            s += 1
            x = (3 * x + 1) // 2
        else:
            x = x // 2
    return s


def noncontracting_classes(k: int) -> List[int]:
    """Residues r < 2^k with 2^k <= 3^{s_k(r)}: the classes a scale-k sieve
    must examine."""
    return [r for r in range(2 ** k) if 2 ** k <= 3 ** odd_step_count(k, r)]


def demo_scale_sieve() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5. THE SCALE-k SIEVE: 2^k <= 3^{s_k(r)} AND VANISHING DENSITY")
    print("=" * 74)

    print("  Scale 2, class by class:")
    for r in range(4):
        s = odd_step_count(2, r)
        print(f"        r = {r}:  s_2(r) = {s},  4 <= 3^{s} = {3 ** s}"
              f"  -> {'NON-CONTRACTING' if 4 <= 3 ** s else 'contracting'}")
    print(f"        non-contracting classes at scale 2 = {noncontracting_classes(2)}"
          "   <- the mod-4 sieve, confirmed optimal")

    print("\n  Density of the examined residue classes as the scale grows:")
    print(f"    {'k':>4}  {'|NC_k|':>10}  {'2^k':>10}  {'density':>10}  "
          f"{'inputs per 10^6 certified':>26}")
    for k in range(2, 19):
        nc = len(noncontracting_classes(k))
        density = nc / 2 ** k
        print(f"    {k:>4}  {nc:>10}  {2 ** k:>10}  {density:>10.5f}  "
              f"{int(density * 10 ** 6):>26}")
    print("\n  The density is not monotone in k (the threshold k log2/log3 crosses")
    print("  integers irregularly), but along any residue class of k it decreases;")
    print("  e.g. for k = 4, 7, 10, 13, 16:")
    subseq = [(k, len(noncontracting_classes(k)) / 2 ** k) for k in (4, 7, 10, 13, 16)]
    print("        " + "  ".join(f"k={k}: {d:.4f}" for k, d in subseq))

    print("\n  Non-contraction requires s_k(r) >= k log2/log3 = 0.6309 k, while a")
    print("  random residue has s_k ~ Binomial(k, 1/2) with mean 0.5 k, so the")
    print("  density tends to 0: for every eps > 0 some scale certifies [1,B]")
    print("  from fewer than eps*B examined inputs, for all large B.")

    # Empirical soundness check of the scale-k sieve for a few k.
    print("\n  Empirical soundness of the scale-k sieve on [1,20000]:")
    for k in (2, 4, 6, 8):
        must_check = [n for n in range(1, 20001) if iterate(accelerated, k, n) >= n]
        ok = all(reaches_one(500, n) for n in must_check)
        covered = all(reaches_one(500, n) for n in range(1, 20001))
        print(f"        k = {k:>2}: examined {len(must_check):>6} of 20000 inputs "
              f"({100 * len(must_check) / 20000:5.2f}%), "
              f"examined all certified: {ok}, whole range holds: {covered}")
    print()


def iterate(f: Callable[[int], int], k: int, n: int) -> int:
    """The k-fold iterate of f applied to n."""
    x = n
    for _ in range(k):
        x = f(x)
    return x


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The learning dichotomy
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_learning_dichotomy() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. THE LEARNING DICHOTOMY: SAME EVIDENCE, OPPOSITE CONCLUSIONS")
    print("=" * 74)

    period = 6
    horizon = 60

    def target(n: int) -> bool:
        return n % period in (1, 2, 5)

    evidence: Dict[int, bool] = {k: target(k) for k in range(1, period + 1)}
    print(f"  Evidence: the values of a predicate at 1..{period} -> "
          f"{[int(evidence[k]) for k in range(1, period + 1)]}\n")

    # Unrestricted class: count hypotheses consistent with the evidence, as a
    # function of how far beyond the window we look.
    print("  Unrestricted hypothesis class - hypotheses consistent with the")
    print("  evidence, distinguishable on the next m inputs:")
    for m in (1, 2, 4, 8):
        print(f"        m = {m:>2}:  {2 ** m:>6} consistent hypotheses")
    print("        (2^aleph_0 = the continuum in the limit)\n")

    # Periodic class: enumerate all period-`period` predicates consistent with
    # the evidence and check they all agree on [1, horizon].
    consistent: List[Tuple[bool, ...]] = []
    for mask in range(2 ** period):
        pattern = tuple(bool((mask >> i) & 1) for i in range(period))

        def hyp(n: int, pattern: Tuple[bool, ...] = pattern) -> bool:
            return pattern[n % period]

        if all(hyp(k) == evidence[k] for k in range(1, period + 1)):
            consistent.append(pattern)

    def behaviour(pattern: Tuple[bool, ...]) -> Tuple[bool, ...]:
        return tuple(pattern[n % period] for n in range(1, horizon + 1))

    behaviours = {behaviour(pat) for pat in consistent}
    print(f"  Period-{period} hypothesis class - consistent hypotheses: "
          f"{len(consistent)}")
    print(f"        distinct behaviours on [1,{horizon}]: {len(behaviours)}"
          "   <- the version space is a singleton")

    # Sharpness: T-1 samples do not suffice.
    print(f"\n  Sharpness: with only {period - 1} samples (1..{period - 1}) the two")
    print("  period-T hypotheses  p = true  and  q(k) = (k mod T != 0)  agree,")
    print("  and differ at T:")
    p_vals = [True for k in range(1, period)]
    q_vals = [k % period != 0 for k in range(1, period)]
    print(f"        agree on [1,{period - 1}] : {p_vals == q_vals}")
    print(f"        differ at {period}         : {True != (period % period != 0)}")
    print(f"        => sample complexity of the period-{period} class is exactly {period}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    print()
    print("#" * 74)
    print("#  CERTIFIED EVIDENCE - numerical companion".ljust(73) + "#")
    print("#  what bounded verification proves, and what it provably cannot"
          .ljust(73) + "#")
    print("#" * 74)
    print()
    demo_reflection()
    demo_insufficiency()
    demo_descent()
    demo_collatz()
    demo_scale_sieve()
    demo_learning_dichotomy()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("SUMMARY")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("  * A bounded check is exactly the bounded statement: sound, complete,")
    print("    gluable, and refutation-complete on finite windows.")
    print("  * No finite window is sound for a universal statement; the version")
    print("    space after any check has the cardinality of the continuum.")
    print("  * A finite window plus a well-founded reduction is a SOUND AND")
    print("    COMPLETE proof system; ten inputs give n^5 = n (mod 10) and three")
    print("    inputs give the semigroup <3,5> with gap set {1,2,4,7}.")
    print("  * The mod-4 sieve is exactly optimal at its scale; higher scales")
    print("    drive the examined fraction to zero; early stopping and balanced")
    print("    evaluation carry the certified Collatz bound from 20 to 131072.")
    print("  * Evidence is worthless or conclusive according to the hypothesis")
    print("    class, never according to the amount of computation.")
    print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
